articles.title: Costa Rican foreign minister dismissed after president misses ‘Shield of Americas’ meeting in NYC
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: Costa Rica’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Manuel Tovar, was dismissed from his post last week by the country’s president Laura Fernández. Tovar was considered one of the “heavyweights” of the country’s dominant political faction, having previously served as Minister of Commerce under President Rodrigo Chávez. The decision was made by Fernández on September 24, because, according to a statement, her foreign minister failed to inform her of an invitation to a meeting held in New York City aimed at strengthening the so-called Shield of the Americas. Shield of the Americas is a political-military alliance led by Donald Trump that seeks to secure Washington’s geopolitical leadership in the region, and which right-wing and far-right Latin American governments have joined enthusiastically. Right-wing President Fernández said that failing to report such an important meeting constituted an act of negligence on Tovar’s part. The Costa Rican president also said that Shield of the Americas is a “fundamental platform in the fight against drug trafficking and organized crime.” The president did not travel to the United States to deliver her speech at the UN General Assembly because she was on an official visit to Colombia with her counterpart, the far-right Abelardo de la Espriella. The Costa Rican presidency reported that the invitation – which was not extended to her – came from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio himself. Several heads of state from Shield of the Americas member states participated, including Javier Milei of Argentina, José Antonio Kast of Chile, Rodrigo Paz of Bolivia, Daniel Noboa of Ecuador, Irfaan Ali of Guyana, Nasry Asfura of Honduras, Santiago Peña of Paraguay, Luis Abinader of the Dominican Republic, and Keiko Fujimori of Peru, among others. In this regard, Fernández publicly apologized to the US ambassador to the Central American country, Melinda Hildebrand: “I reiterate to your country my firm and resolute commitment to continue supporting the Shield of the Americas alliance… I regret my absence… The failure to forward that invitation from your government to me did not go unnoticed, and today the foreign minister of the Republic was dismissed,” which clearly demonstrates the enormous importance San José attaches to an invitation from Washington. Tovar’s dismissal comes on the heels of a series of dismissals of key ministers in Fernández’s government, a development the opposition has used to highlight a certain instability in the very young administration. “We are concerned about serious foreign policy mistakes that need to be corrected… Second, we are concerned about the stability of the cabinet: in less than five months, five senior officials – including ministers and deputy ministers – have already been dismissed. That instability is not in her best interest, nor in that of her government or Costa Rica,” said the leader of the National Liberation Party caucus. For his part, the former foreign minister did not explain the reasons behind his decision not to inform Fernández about the invitation. In a post on X, he said briefly : “I thank Laura Fernández for the opportunity to serve the Costa Rican people from the Casa Amarilla, and I wish her every success as President of the Republic for the good of the country. Finally, I would like to commend the team at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for the passion and dedication with which they undertake every mission on behalf of the country. To them, I offer my eternal gratitude. I accept this moment with great peace of mind. I will always stand by the just causes of the Costa Rican people and the international community.” The reasons behind Tovar’s decision remain unknown, although several sectors of the opposition have raised suspicions about an alleged ulterior motive on Fernández’s part for not attending the Shield of the Americas meeting – which, if true, could reveal political and diplomatic contradictions deeper than they might appear at first glance.

articles.title: Movement for the release of former PM Imran Khan heats up in Pakistan
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), the country’s main opposition party, announced a long march to the capital, Islamabad, on Sunday, October 4, as part of its ongoing nationwide movement to demand the release of its leader and former Prime Minister Imran Khan. The march, which was originally scheduled to be held on Sunday, September 27, starting from Peshawar, was postponed on Friday after the party’s top leadership decided it needed more time to mobilize to face the state’s preparations to block it. Thousands of people have been taking to the streets in different parts of the country demanding the immediate release of Khan, his wife Bushra Bibi, and other party leaders. Khan’s party and supporters have also accused the Shehbaz Sharif-led coalition government in the country of deliberately ignoring Khan’s bad health condition and trying to “slowly kill him in prison” by keeping him in solitary confinement. They have also alleged that Khan has been denied access to his family members and party colleagues in Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail for almost six months now and demanded that he be transferred out of the jail to a private hospital. State repression Meanwhile, the security forces have fortified the capital, blocking all the ways leading to the capital with shipping containers and large deployments after the government called the protests illegal and threatened consequences for the PTI leadership. Pakistan’s Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had earlier called the march a failure and “a drama” and warned that if the PTI does not abandon its plan to go to Islamabad the state will find a “permanent solution” to stop them. The security forces had arrested a large number of PTI leaders and workers in order to derail the protests. The PTI last week said that even its elected members of the National Assembly were arrested. Three of Khan’s sisters Aleema, Uzma, and Noreen Khan were also arrested by the Pakistani authorities last week and jailed for 30 days on charges of being an alleged “threat to public order.” The PTI released a statement on Monday, September 28, claiming Khan’s sisters have not been allowed to meet their family members or lawyers at Kot Lakhpat Jail in Lahore. Calling the situation of their incarceration “alarming” and a violation of their fundamental rights. The previous mobilization to Islamabad in November 2024 had also witnessed large-scale state repression leading to clashes between the security forces and the PTI workers. Over a dozen people, including four security officials, were killed in those clashes. Three years of incarceration Khan, largely considered the most popular political leader in Pakistan’s politics today, was first arrested almost a year after he was ousted from his Prime Minister’s post in May 2023. He led the Pakistan government from August 2018 to April 2022. The interim government that assumed power after his removal filed over a hundred cases against Khan, accusing him of the misuse of power, corruption, and violence against the security forces during the May 9, 2023 protests. However, he was released after a court ruled his arrest was illegal only to be arrested again on August 5, this time after a district court sentenced him to three years in prison in the Toshakhana case, related to the state department that stores valuable gifts given to Pakistani officials by foreign dignitaries. Later his wife Bushra Bibi was also arrested. Though a higher court later overturned his conviction, he and his wife have remained in Adiala Jail facing charges and even convictions in several other cases. Many leaders in Khan’s party, PTI, were either arrested or forced to denounce the party and politics in public altogether. Despite the fact that the PTI was blocked from contesting national elections in February 2024, it emerged as the largest opposition group in the country’s National Assembly after it decided to field its candidates as independents. PTI and Khan’s supporters maintain that the cases against Khan and his wife were politically motivated and fake. Ammar Ali Jan, leader of the Left wing Haqooq-e-Khalq Party (HKP) and a member of the Tehreek-i-Tahaffuz Ayeen-i-Pakistan (Movement to Save Pakistan’s Constitution or TTAP) formed as a broader alliance to fight for Khan’s release has condemned the continued incarceration of Khan and the repression of movements for his release. He also questioned the state’s narrative about the failure of the movement, pointing out how it has made every effort to oppress it, including the arrests and fortification of the capital.

articles.title: Brazil’s movements occupy streets across the country in defense of democracy and Lula’s candidacy
articles.author: Brasil de Fato
articles.content: Militants and supporters of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva participated, this Sunday, September 27, in demonstrations as part of the national mobilization “Let’s go, Lula,” held a week before the first round of elections. In Rio de Janeiro, “CarnaLula 2026” spanned the length of Copacabana beach. With a microphone, PT Senate candidate Benedita da Silva spoke about the importance of Carnival as an expression of popular culture and called on those present to also vote for a progressive bloc in the Rio de Janeiro Legislative Assembly and the Federal Chamber of Deputies. She reinforced the discourse that, in this election, not only democracy is at stake, but also national sovereignty . “We will not be anyone’s backyard,” she repeated Lula’s phrase. Read more: Brazil’s presidential campaign heats up In São Paulo, the event began with Carnival parades, circus performances, and bike rides on Paulista Avenue, where candidates gave speeches in defense of democracy. “Denialism will not prevail,” said Senate candidate Simone Tebet. Federal deputy Erika Hilton echoed Tebet, speaking about the importance of electing candidates who will steer Brazil away from fascism and who are in favor of the working class, as well as defending the end of the 6×1 work schedule . Also present at the event, actor Humberto Carrão told Brasil de Fato that he urged voters to decide the presidential election in the first round. The capital of Minas Gerais, Belo Horizonte, was one of the cities with the largest number of activities in support of Lula’s re-election. Among them was a flag-waving demonstration in the city center, where hundreds of activists unfurled a banner that read “Lula of Brazil.” In a review of the event, Pedro Martins, a member of the Alvorada collective, one of the organizers of the action, spoke of the need to occupy the streets. “It was a spectacular event, with all the social movements gathered. This week was an important week, showing that we need to go to the streets, and only in this way can we turn the vote around and achieve victory,” he told Brasil de Fato . In Florianópolis and Curitiba, supporters held a bike ride carrying flags in defense of Lula’s candidacy. In Brasília, the gathering was on the Eixão, a fast road that connects the Plano Piloto from north to south. Lula’s campaign reported that the day’s events were organized in a decentralized manner, with more than 500 activities planned across the 27 state capitals and hundreds of municipalities. The program included walks, motorcades, leaflet distribution, and cultural performances. First published by Brasil de Fato in Portuguese.

articles.title: Forcible Eviction of 87-Year-Old Madrid Woman Sparks Protest Encampment over Spain’s Housing Crisis
articles.content: The eviction of 87-year-old María del Carmen Abascal Martín in Madrid, after an investment fund bought her apartment building and more than tripled her rent, has become a symbol of Spain’s rising cost of living and sparked nationwide protests against corporate greed and wealth inequality. Over 600 protesters are now camped outside Madrid’s regional government headquarters demanding new tenant protections. “What we have is a lot of furious people, enraged people, that are demanding from the government and from the public institutions that they give us give us some sort of solution,” says Sabina Carrau, a spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants’ Union, which is supporting the “Maricarmen decree” named after Abascal, set to be debated by Spain’s government this week. Housing in Spain, as in much of the world, “is really connected to tourism, really connected to having and buying a house to make a speculation,” says socialist parliamentarian Tesh Sidi, who is calling instead for the guaranteed right to housing and “the right to have an affordable life.” Sidi, the only Sahrawi member of the Spanish parliament, also comments on Spain’s colonial relationship to Western Sahara and the state of Sahrawi rights and self-determination.

articles.title: “Britain’s Gaza Secrets Exposed”: How U.K. Downplayed Israeli Crimes to Keep Selling Weapons
articles.content: A new documentary titled Britain’s Gaza Secrets Exposed reveals new details about the U.K. government’s internal response to alleged Israeli war crimes in Gaza. Presented by journalist Ramita Navai and produced by Ben De Pear for Channel 4’s investigative program Dispatches , the documentary examines government records, some newly publicized, to show how the United Kingdom ignored or concealed mounting evidence of Israel’s genocidal actions in Gaza after the October 7 attacks. “We were looking at how our country, which prides itself on having an ethical foreign policy and as being one of the supporting members of the United Nations on human rights, was able to keep selling arms,” says De Pear. “And basically, what we found was a doctored process … It’s quite extraordinary the level of duplicity that was going on in order for us to keep selling Israel arms.” Ben De Pear also produced the 2025 BAFTA -winning documentary Gaza: Doctors Under Attack , which the British Broadcasting Corporation, or BBC , initially commissioned but later refused to air. Gaza: Doctors Under Attack was broadcast instead by Channel 4.

articles.title: “Valley of Death”: Sharon Weinberger on Big Tech, AI Warfare & the CIA’s Secret Backing of Steve Jobs
articles.content: Longtime national security reporter Sharon Weinberger’s new book, Valley of Death: How Big Tech Is Fueling the Future of War , follows the rise of the military-industrial complex in Silicon Valley, where defense technology companies, like Palantir, Anduril and SpaceX, and their billionaire founders, are increasingly shaping U.S. foreign policy. Weinberger explains that because “the government doesn’t own the underlying technology” peddled by “this new class of entrepreneurs,” these companies have upended the traditional procurement relationship between the U.S. government and older defense firms, and now unilaterally control access to the new weapons and systems — including drones and artificial intelligence — used in modern warfare.

articles.title: A Beacon for the Socialist Revolution: The Political Writings of Rosa Luxemburg
articles.author: Panagiotis Sotiris
articles.content: Rosa Luxemburg, The Complete Works of Rosa Luxemburg , Volume III: Political Writings 1, On Revolution, 1897-1905 , eds. Peter Hudis and Sandra Rein; trans. George Shriver, Alicja Mann, and Henry Holland (London and New York: Verso Books, 2019, paperback, 2022). 592 pp.; Volume IV: Political Writings 2, On Revolution, 1906-1909 , eds. Peter Hudis and Sandra Rein; trans. Jacob Blumenfeld, Nicholas Grey, Henry Holland, Zachary King, Manuella Kölke, and Joseph Muller (London and New York: Verso Books, 2022; paperback, 2023). 576 pp; Volume V: Political Writings 1, On Revolution, 1910-1919 , eds. Paul Le Blanc and Helen C. Scott; trans. Jacob Blumenfeld, Mathias Foit, Nicholas Gray, Henry Holland, Zachary King and Manuela Kölke (London and New York: Verso Books, 2024; paperback, 2026). 512 pp. Reviewed by Ronald Grigor Suny [1] Truly a labour of love, as well as sincere political and scholarly commitment, dedicated investigators of the history of revolutionary Social Democracy have been working for decades collecting, translating, and publishing the writings of one of the most prolific and insightful Marxist thinkers of the twentieth century, Rosa Luxemburg (1871-1919). These documents not readily available to English readers began to appear in large volumes in 2013 and have now reached the third volume of the political writings in a paperback edition. Reading through these weighty tomes, it becomes clear that Luxemburg, born in the aftermath of one revolution, the Paris Commune, and murdered in another revolutionary upsurge, was a woman of strong views never reluctant to express them no matter the effect on personal relationships. The red thread through her work on revolution was her deep commitment to the initiative of the working class to carry out the revolutions against the hegemony of capitalism. Her articles vibrate with her energy and passion for the labour movement and vividly demonstrate that a major shift in Marxist perceptions occurred with the explosion of worker activity in the most backward of European powers, Russia, beginning in late 1904 and through the next several years. In the aftermath of the struggles against the revisionism of Eduard Bernstein and the pervasive parliamentarism of the majority of German Social Democrats, Luxemburg and other critics of gradualist reformism were recharged by the men and — she emphasises – proletarian women fighting for democracy in Russia. “The starting point for the next wave of revolution had shifted from the west to east” (III, p. 50). What has been called “the revolution of 1905” was revolutionary in the intensity and duration of labour activity that forced the autocrat to concede a kind of limited “constitution” granting some rights to his people in October 1905. But the regime was not overthrown and would rebound, unwilling to give up its claim to be autocratic and searching desperately to take back what it had been forced to grant. Before Lenin, who came late to appreciate the spontaneity that workers would display, Luxemburg celebrated the spontaneous uprising of the Russian proletariat and its “accidental leader”, the priest Father Georgii Gapon. Social Democrats both inspired and led the movement, she agreed, but they had been surprised by the independent action of the proletariat. While “it was the spirit of Marx that struck the first great blow in the streets of Petersburg”, Russian Social Democrats “had to adjust themselves everywhere to pressure from the workers” (III, pp. 58, 45). Marxists had to rethink their ideas about Russia and learn the lesson of revolutionary optimism presented by the Russian proletariat. Russia was showing both the necessity and meaning of the “bourgeois revolution”, for “the working class is not the means to an end – political liberty – but political liberty is a means to the end of the emancipation of the working class” (III, p. 50). The “cause of freedom and of social progress everywhere now lies with the class-conscious proletariat,” she proclaimed. “And it is in good hands!” (III, p. 63). Even as the revolution succumbed to brutal repression by the tsarist government, Luxemburg lauded the strategic innovations of the Russian workers. They had moved a bourgeois-democratic revolution toward a proletarian-socialist one by transcending from parliamentary struggles to the creation of “a new method of struggle”, “the revolutionary mass strike” (III, p. 475). The great dilemma of the Russian Revolution, both in 1905 and 1917, was that the proletariat was the instrument that would open the way for the bourgeois-democratic revolution, but a truly socialist revolution was impossible in Russia without a long period of capitalist development. Socialism could not be imposed by a minority; only by an immense majority. As the editors of volume IV point out, “Herein lay the dual character of the Russian Revolution. It was proletarian in form, but bourgeois-democratic in content” (IV, p. xxvi). The proletariat fought for the maximal democracy in order that it could instrumentalise bourgeois liberties for the struggle against the bourgeoisie. Luxemburg understood a great truth in European history, that the reaching toward democracy was, in fact, the achievement not only of the limited political advances of the liberal bourgeoisie but of the sustained struggle of the working people. [2] An early critic of Lenin’s controversial pamphlet What Is to Be Done? (1902), Luxemburg had grown critical of Georgii Plekhanov’s labelling the Bolshevik leader a Blanquist, that is, someone favouring the seizure of power by a small clique in a conspiratorial coup d’état. Life, and a revolution, had intervened, and Lenin had responded enthusiastically to the self-activisation of Russian, Polish, Georgian, and other workers. He was himself annoyed by the dogmatic adherence of some his comrades to what they believed was his formulation of the party leading the workers since they were unable to come to revolutionary consciousness without the help of party intellectuals. Whereas, in 1902, he emphasised the power of bourgeois cultural hegemony that pushed workers toward accommodation with capitalism, impressed by the militancy of Petersburg, Baku, and other workers, Lenin wrote three years later, “The working class is instinctively, spontaneously Social-Democratic, and the more than ten years of work of Social Democracy has done a great deal to turn this spontaneity into consciousness.” [3] In the heat of the revolution, many Social Democrats papered over their differences and adopted more radical strategies. After a stint in prison and long conversations with Lenin and other leading Bolsheviks then living in Finland, Luxemburg composed her major theoretical and strategic intervention into the debates with the long essay, “The Mass Strike, the Political Parties, and the Trade Unions”, which later was praised by leading Bolsheviks. She set out to analyse what the Russian Revolution had taught Social Democrats about the current usefulness of the mass strike, which Marx and Engels had derided as an apolitical, anarchist method of struggle. Her audience was primarily in Germany, where she hoped to convince her comrades and the workers that, in the moment, 1906, when the revolutionary wave appeared to recede, the struggle must combine both politics and mass action. In her speeches to the congress of Russian Social Democrats later that year, she sided more with the Bolsheviks in their suspicions about the bourgeoisie than with the Mensheviks ready to temper their radicalism in order not to frighten the liberals. While most German Social Democrats were suspicious of her militancy, she remained confident that the role of Social Democrats was to develop the class consciousness that was inherent in the spontaneous actions of the proletariat. Workers might make the wrong choices at times, but their required goal is the broadest democracy in which their consciousness can flourish. Where she would differ from the Bolsheviks a little over a decade later was that she objected to the idea that there were alternative, non-democratic paths to socialism. The anticipated proletarian majority, however, never manifested itself in the history of the next century, except in small fleeting occasions and on the local rather than national level. Her faith in the “masses”, as she referred to working people, never faltered, her optimism rooted in a vision of the future. There is nothing more changeable than human psychology. That’s especially because the psyche of the masses, like … the eternal sea, always bears within it every latent possibility: deathly stillness and raging storm, the basest cowardice and the wildest heroism. The masses are always what they must be according to the circumstances of the times, and they are always on the verge of becoming something totally different from what they seem to be. (V, p. xvii.) The mass strike was a weapon in the arsenal of Social Democracy that would accompany the parliamentarism of her more moderate comrades like Karl Kautsky but represented the revolutionary expression of the working people’s instinctual resistance against the mute compulsions and overt repressions of capitalism. Luxemburg focused on the maximum programme of Social Democracy, the socialist revolution, in anticipation that moments would unexpectedly arise to jump beyond the minimum programme of reform. Socialists in the years before World War I, like those in the present day, were faced by the dilemma that the state and capital were powerful enough to crush the working class should it seriously threaten the social order. August Bebel, Friedrich Engels, and Kautsky all cautioned against insurrectionism. 1848 and 1871 were in the past, and 1917 was not yet on the horizon. Observing the technological advances in military science that served to strengthen the repressive power of the bourgeois state, Engels warned that “‘the powers-that-be’ positively want to get us to go where the guns shoot and the sabers slash” (V, p. xxiii). Luxemburg, however, had come to realise the leadership of the German Social-Democratic Party had become an obstacle to the revolution, and this would be culminate in its capitulation to the imperial regime on 4 August 1914, when the majority voted to support the war effort. The fateful decision of Social-Democratic parties on both sides of the War to act in concert with their governments rather than fulfil the promises repeated in international congresses that the workers’ opposition would prevent war irrevocably fractured the unity of the Left. In the next few years, the radical Left gained support as the War dragged on, and Luxemburg greeted the outbreak of revolution in Russia in February 1917, as “the first conspicuous expression of proletarian class politics since the bankruptcy of international socialism at the outbreak of the World War, and thus the first advance for peace of world-historical significance” (V, p. 151). By August, she had essentially adopted the Bolshevik position on state power in Russia, writing in Spartacus that the coalition government in Russia, which allied bourgeois representatives with socialists, was “a compromise that, like all compromises, is condemned to ultimate fiasco. The new coalition ministry will, by virtue of internal logical development, sooner or later have to give way to a purely socialist government, that is to say, the actual and formal dictatorship of the proletariat” (V, p. 154). Two months later, the most dedicatedly anti-war party, the Bolsheviks, basing their right to rule on the democratically-elected soviets, came to power. With a militant workers’ party at the helm of the largest country on the globe, a definitive dye had been cast. Luxemburg focused primarily on the issue of ending the War, which would begin with the Russians but required the German workers to complete. At the time of Germany’s triumphs in the East, on the eve of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in 1918 and the creation of German satellite statelets governed by anti-Bolsheviks, she wrote, “The German workers are now called upon to carry the tidings of the revolution and of peace from East to West. Here, no pursing of the lips will do—here, you have to blow the whistle” (V, p. 169). She framed the Russian Revolution as the clearest evidence of the failure of German Social Democracy led by those like Kautsky who had functioned “as an ideological cover for German imperialism’s campaign of conquest” (V, p. 215). Late in 1918, just months before she was assassinated in Berlin during the Spartacist revolt, Luxemburg worked on an unfinished manuscript that represents her last musings on the Russian Revolution and the policies of the Bolsheviks. She began by linking the origins and potential success of the revolution to the international conjuncture of the War, its continuity with the lessons of the revolution of 1905, and its growth from bourgeois revolution to a socialist revolution that extended beyond the boundaries of Russia. She rejected the overly-cautious Mensheviks, who allied with bourgeois parties. “Lenin’s party was thus the only one in Russia that had a grasp of the true interests of the revolution in this initial period,” she wrote, “it was the element that drove the revolution forward, being in this sense the only party to pursue a socialist politics” (V, p. 221). Within a few months, the “actual situation in which the Russian Revolution found itself came down… to the following alternative: victory of the counterrevolution or dictatorship of the proletariat—i.e., Kaledin or Lenin…. Their October uprising not only salvaged the Russian Revolution, it also salvaged the honor of international socialism” (V, p. 221). Along with defending a democratic road to socialism, she focused on crucial errors that she claimed were made by the Bolsheviks. “Lenin’s agrarian reform has engendered in the countryside a new and powerful popular stratum of adversaries of socialism, whose resistance will be much more dangerous and tenacious than that previously offered by the aristocratic owners of large estates” (V, p. 237). Concessions to the peasants were matched by his policy toward non-Russian peoples. A fierce opponent of nationalisms, Luxemburg rejected Lenin’s slogan of national self-determination of nations. On the one hand, they have displayed their profound disdain for the Constituent Assembly, for universal suffrage, for freedom of the press and freedom of assembly—in short, for the entire apparatus of basic democratic freedoms of the popular masses that, taken together, formed the “right of self-determination” in Russia itself. On the other hand, however, they have treated the right of self-determination of nations as a jewel of democratic politics, for the sake of which all practical considerations of real critique were to be silenced. (V, p. 228.) In contrast to Trotsky’s defence of non-democratic methods, Luxemburg singled out the importance of democracy for the education and advancement of the proletariat. Trotsky, she wrote, held that: Owing to the open and direct struggle for power, the working people acquire much political experience in a short time and pass rapidly from one stage to the next in their development. The ponderous machinery of democratic institutions lags behind this evolution all the more, the bigger the country and the less perfect its technical apparatus. (V, p. 235.) She passionately disagreed: the remedy that Trotsky and Lenin have discovered—the elimination of democracy as such—is worse than the evil that it is supposed to prevent, for it occludes the very living source alone from which any correction of all the deficiencies inherent within social institutions can emanate. That source is none other than the active, uninhibited, vigorous political life of the broadest masses of the people. (V, p. 237.) Luxemburg understood that the resistance of the bourgeoisie had to be smashed “with an iron fist,” as the Bolsheviks had done following the October Revolution, but such temporary measures did not then eliminate the need for the expansion of democracy enfranchising all. Lenin and Trotsky’s choices, in Luxemburg’s formulation, were detrimental to the creation of a public sphere essential for the education and development of the proletariat (V, p. 239). Democracy was not a luxury but a necessity. [I]t is evident that, by its very nature, socialism cannot be imposed—it cannot be introduced by ukase. It has as its prerequisite a series of coercive measures—against property, etc. The negative—the dismantling of what exists—can be decreed; the positive cannot. It is a terra incognita…. [Lenin] errs completely in the means that he employs… Decrees, the dictatorial powers of factory supervisors, draconian punishments, the reign of terror — these are all mere palliatives. The only way to a renaissance is the school of public life itself, the most unrestricted and broadest democracy, public opinion. In contrast, the very reign of terror itself has a demoralizing effect. (V, p. 242.) She predicted correctly that, “with the stifling of political life in the country as a whole, vitality within the soviets will also necessarily tend to wane. Without general elections, without unrestricted freedom of the press and of assembly, without a free struggle of opinions, vitality withers away in each public institution—it becomes a pseudo-vitality in which bureaucracy is the only remaining active element” (V, p. 243). And then, powerfully, she points to a future that she will not live to see. Public life gradually falls into a slumber, a few dozen party leaders with inexhaustible energy and boundless idealism direct and govern; among the latter, a dozen outstanding minds are, in reality, the ones that lead, and an elite from within the working class is occasionally mustered in order to applaud the speeches of the leaders and to show unanimous approval for the resolutions drafted by them. (V, p. 243.) Ending her essay, Luxemburg praised the Bolsheviks for demonstrating that they “could achieve everything that a genuinely revolutionary party is capable of accomplishing within the limits of historical possibilities. They should attempt to perform miracles…. In Russia, the problem could be posed; it could not be solved there. And, in this sense , the future everywhere belongs to ‘Bolshevism’” (V, p. 245). Luxemburg’s faith in the spontaneity of working people appears to have proven even more prescient in our own time. Engels’s warning about the state-capital hegemon’s brutality suggests that alternative avenues to undermining the structures of power are required along with political participation in whatever democratic practices remain. Gramsci’s war of manoeuvre involving revolutionary political struggles, even direct attacks against the state, must be accompanied by a war of position, that is, the seemingly more tedious, gradual building up of the labour movement, its organisations, and its hegemony in the public and social spheres. Even in the most entrenched capitalist monolith, the United States, spontaneity without warning erupts – in occupations of Wall Street, Black Lives Matter, climate change activists, the streets of Minnesota, and pro-Palestinian encampments. Democratic socialists challenge the pusillanimous Democratic Party establishment. The state appears bewildered and turns to novel forms of repression. Liberals fret that the institutions will not hold, the rule of law will be undercut. Confused by their visceral reformism, they cannot face up to the lessons learned from the last century. The Soviet experiment taught us that there is no socialism without democracy, and the impasse of American neoliberal capitalism and bourgeois democracy teaches us, there is no democracy without socialism. At the supposed end of history, Luxemburg remains right. [1] Ronald Grigor Suny is William H. Sewell Jr. Distinguished University Professor Emeritus of History and Political Science at the University of Michigan and Professor Emeritus of History and Political Science at the University of Chicago. He is the author of, among many works, The Baku Commune, 1917-1918: Class and Nationality in the Russian Revolution (Princeton University Press, 1972); The Revenge of the Past: Nationalism, Revolution, and the Collapse of the Soviet Union (Stanford University Press, 1993); The Soviet Experiment: Russia, the USSR, and the Successor States (Oxford University Press, 1998, 2011); “They Can Live in the Desert But Nowhere Else”: A History of the Armenian Genocide (Princeton University Press, 2015); Stalin: Passage to Revolution (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2020). [2] The importance of workers, the labor movement, and Social Democracy in the struggle of democracy is the central argument of Geoff Eley’s Forging Democracy: The History of the Left in Europe, 1850-2000 (New York: Oxford University Press, 2002). [3] V.I. Lenin, “O reorganizatsii partii,” Polnoe sobranie sochinenii (5th edition: Moscow: Izdatel’stvo politicheskoi literatury, 1958–1965), XII, p. 86. articles.title: 77 countries walk out during Netanyahu’s UN speech
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: Israel continues to face isolation in international forums as it continues its multi-front war on the peoples of West Asia. On Thursday, September 24, delegations from at least 77 countries walked out or left their seats vacant during the address of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. The move was interpreted as opposition to Israel’s three-year genocidal aggression on Gaza, and atrocities across multiple parts of West Asia. Arab nations that walked out included: Algeria, Comoros, Egypt, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, Mauritania, Oman, Palestine, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, Tunisia and Yemen. Asian states involved: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Brunei, Darussalam, Indonesia, Iran, Kyrgyzstan, Malaysia, Maldives, Myanmar, North Korea, Pakistan, Türkiye, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. From Africa the following left the chamber: Angola, Botswana, Central African Republic, Chad, Congo (Republic of the), Democratic Republic of the Congo, Djibouti, Equatorial Guinea, Eritrea, Eswatini, Kenya, Lesotho, Liberia, Madagascar, Mozambique, Namibia, Niger, Senegal, South Africa and Uganda. Countries of Latin America and the Caribbean: Antigua and Barbuda, Bahamas, Barbados, Belize, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Cuba, Dominica, Guyana, Nicaragua, Panama, Peru, Saint Lucia, Suriname, and Venezuela. European countries: Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ireland, North Macedonia, San Marino, Slovenia and Spain. From Oceania: Tonga and Tuvalu. Meanwhile, thousands of protesters took to the streets of New York City, where the UN headquarters is located, to protest Netanyahu’s visit and address, calling for US officials to comply with the warrant issued for his arrest from the International Criminal Court. Read more: ICC issues arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant as the genocide continues in Gaza Netanyahu defies the world, vows to continue Israel’s multi-front regional war Netanyahu began his defiant, combatant speech by calling the departing delegations “moral cowards”. “If there are any other moral cowards who haven’t yet left this hall, please do so now,” the Israeli PM said, addressing an almost empty chamber. During the rest of his speech, which lasted for around 40 minutes, he defended Israel’s military campaigns – including the strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities – and vowed “to continue to win” Israel’s muti-front regional war, claiming his government has “no other choice”. Netanyahu categorically rejected international accusations of genocide in Gaza, labeling them “the greatest lie of the century”. He sharply criticized his vocal opponents, naming Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and the government of Qatar. Furthermore, Netanyahu downplayed the deadly impact of Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank by describing the perpetrators as a “handful of young juvenile delinquents, about 150 in number, who go throw stones, who chop down olive trees, and occasionally light some fires.” He also minimized the total number of Palestinian casualties resulting from settler attacks saying “maybe two or three dead” per year, although the UN reported in August that at least 23 Palestinians were killed and more than 1,040 others were injured in the context of settler attacks since the beginning of 2026. Responding to statements made by Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa concerning Syria’s sovereignty over the Golan Heights, Netanyahu firmly asserted Israel’s permanent claim over the territory, invoking a biblical narrative. “Jews have been on the Golan Heights since the days of Moses,” Netanyahu declared, asking Al-Sharaa to “read it in the Bible”. Abbas continues to appeal to the US despite its sanctions on PA For the second year in a row, the US State Department has denied entry visas to the President of the Palestinian Authority (PA) Mahmoud Abbas and a high-level delegation, preventing them from attending the United Nations General Assembly session in New York. According to media reports , the Trump administration justified the revocation of visas by accusing the PA of pursuing legal action against Israel in international courts, and failing to meet past peace commitments. The decision drew wide international criticism for violating UN host-country agreements. The US action put Abbas on the spot before the Palestinian grassroots, especially as his administration is known for appeasing Washington at the cost of the Palestinian people’s sacrifices. Read more: Abbas sacks head of detainees’ commission for opposing cuts of prisoners and martyrs’ stipends Opening his pre-recorded speech delivered remotely, Abbas strongly condemned the revocation of US visas for Palestinian officials – including himself – as “punitive and unlawful”, rejecting the justifications provided by Washington. He urged the US to lift the sanctions and restrictions it imposed on the PA, resume dialogue, and work alongside the international community to back the two-state solution. Abbas stressed that the PA has fulfilled its governance and reform commitments, and reaffirmed his leadership’s dedication to international law and its ongoing stance against “violence and terrorism”. In terms of the situation on the ground, Abbas cautioned that Palestinians are confronting the most dangerous phase in their modern history. He detailed the repercussions of the ongoing Israeli genocide and the severe humanitarian crisis in Gaza, in addition to settlement expansion, land seizures, and the escalation in settler violence under the protection of Israeli forces in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem. The Palestinian President warned that these systemic practices are designed to fragment the territory and forcibly displace the Palestinian people. “We have, for long, warned the international community through the UN General Assembly and the Security Council that these Israeli policies that operate outside international law will destroy the two-state solution,” Abbas asserted. The head of the PA slammed some countries for their silence and their continued supply of weapons to Israel. While acknowledging the 20-point plan brought forward by US President Donald Trump for post-war Gaza, the related UN Security Council resolution and the Mladenov 15-point roadmap , he lamented the lack of tangible progress and called for the immediate expedition of phase two of the ceasefire deal. Abbas also expressed hope that phase two of the deal would unify Gaza, the West Bank, and Jerusalem under the mandate of the Palestinian state. Concluding his address, Abbas called on Trump to abide by his previous commitments made to Arab and Islamic leaders regarding the prevention of land annexation and forced displacement of the Palestinian people. He further demanded the immediate, unconditional release of more than USD 6 billion in tax revenues withheld by Israel, alongside an end to the financial siege on Palestinian institutions. With regard to the long-awaited legislative elections, Abbas affirmed that it will take place on November 28, followed subsequently by presidential elections. He closed by reiterating the vision of a democratic, unarmed Palestinian state grounded in human rights and the rule of law, living side-by-side with Israel in “mutual security and peace”. Visa revocations show concessions yield zero results, says Omar Assaf Palestinian political activist and former prisoner in Israeli jails, Omar Assaf, argues that the denial of US entry visas to the Palestinian delegation highlights two critical realities. First, it exposes a deep-rooted US hostility toward the Palestinian people and their leadership, actively blocking them from reaching the United Nations to make the World hear their grievances, assert their rights, and bear witness to the crimes of the occupation. Second, it serves as a stark wake-up call for Palestinian leadership that the US administration cannot be relied upon, nor can it be viewed as an honest broker, or a mediator of any kind. From his point of view, the incident makes clear that a policy of concessions, compliance, appeasement, and pleading yields zero results. Instead, the World only respects the language of strength, unity and upholding rights. Consequently, this must serve as a definitive lesson for Palestinians to close ranks under a unified national stance. “We must firmly adhere to our people’s rights, stand resilient against challenges, and confront any aggression targeting our land and existence, including our fundamental right to make our voices heard globally to halt these ongoing crimes,” Assaf emphasized.
